1.pericope_label: Jesus speaks to the multitude and to his disciples of the scribes and Pharisees who sit in Moses seat, bidding them observe what these men say but not do after their works, since they bind heavy burdens and will not move them with one finger

schools.summary: Gill places the address after the priests and Pharisees had left Christ nonplussed and finds two dangers in the moment, that the people having seen their teachers errors detected might conclude there was nothing in religion, or that being overawed by men in Moses chair they might be led into bad principles, the discourse guarding both and clearing Christ of enmity to Moses rightly explained; he restrains the command to observe to what agrees with the chair they sit in, many of their glosses being repugnant to the law, and names the heavy burdens as the traditions of the elders; Calvin states the design more broadly, that the word of God might remain entire amid the noise of combat, since men are prone to dislike the Law and grow wanton through a dissolute pastor example, forming their rulers corrupt manners into a law for themselves, notes that the attack is ordered so that the Law is first vindicated from contempt before the teachers are exposed, and denies that harsh laws are in view in the fourth verse at all, finding the fault in the stern manner of enforcing them.

Henry reads the seat of the Sanhedrim, the standing bench that determined appeals rather than the judges who rode the circuit, and allows the other application to the scribes who expounded the law, since Ezra pulpit of wood is here called Moses seat; he draws two notes from it, that many a good place is filled with bad men, the seat being dishonoured by the men rather than the men honoured by the seat, and that a useful office is not to be abolished because bad men abuse it.

Clarke marks the sharper distinction about the seat, that they sat there formerly by divine appointment and now by divine permission, presses the past tense of the command, whatsoever they have commanded, and suggests a reference to a former period when they taught the way of God in truth, and names the burdens as traditions added without reason, expediency or revelation; Wesley reads the opening word as a turn away from the adversaries, whom he now left to the hardness of their hearts.

Ellicott hears an appeal to the unperverted conscience of the people against the perversions of their guides, observes that Christ closes his public teaching as he began it with a protest against a casuistry that had put the traditions of men in the place of the commandments of God, and finds the lack not in the maxims but in the life, it being one thing to draw fine pictures of virtue and another to live by them; Barnes explains the custom, that they sat to expound the law and rose to read it, so that sitting in the seat means authority to teach, holds that the word all cannot stand unrestricted since Christ himself charges them with teaching against the law, and argues from the apostle words at Jerusalem that the burdens must be the rites of Moses rather than traditions, since Christ would not have bidden the people keep traditions; Robertson calls it the chair of the professor whose function is to interpret Moses, quotes the view that they were heirs of his authority by an unbroken tradition, and says that as teachers they have their place but their practice is not to be copied; Lightfoot takes the seat of the legislative chair rather than the merely doctrinal, so that Christ asserts the authority of the magistrate, and supplies the rabbinic saying that the crafty wicked man is he who prescribes light things to himself and heavy to others.

debates.question: What are the heavy burdens they bind on others?

sides.position: the traditions of the elders, added without reason, expediency or revelation
the rites of Moses, which the apostle said the fathers could not bear, since Christ would not have bidden the people keep traditions
neither; the fault lies not in the laws but in the stern and rigid manner of enforcing them

debates.question: What authority does sitting in Moses seat confer?

sides.position: the authority of the magistrate and the legislative chair, to be obeyed in lawful things
authority to teach and expound the law, nothing more
a seat once held by divine appointment and now only by divine permission

outliers: Calvin alone treats the passage as a problem of order, insisting that the Law be cleared of contempt before its ministers are exposed.
Henry alone turns the abuse of the seat into a rule about offices, that a useful one is not to be abolished because bad men hold it.
themes: a warning given to the crowd rather than the men
an office honourable while its holders are not
obedience with a judgment of discretion
burdens laid on by men who carry none

5.pericope_label: All their works they do to be seen of men, making broad their phylacteries and enlarging the borders of their garments, and they love the uppermost rooms at feasts, the chief seats in the synagogues, greetings in the markets and to be called Rabbi

schools.summary: Gill observes that their prayers, alms and fastings were all performed in public, so that they sought neither the glory of God nor the good of their fellow creatures nor any pleasure to themselves; Calvin takes it further, that whatever is apparently good in such men is hypocritical and worthless, the things they boast of being absolute trifles because they spring from mere ostentation, and an upright worshipper never giving himself to that empty parade, and he presses the prohibition of the title hardest, that the honour belongs to Christ alone and cannot be given to a man without injury to him.

Henry grants that we must do good works which those who see them may glorify God for, but not proclaim them that others may glorify us, noting that in the duties which fall under the eye of men none were so abundant while in the recesses of their hearts they desired to be excused; he reads the original command about the law on hand and forehead as figurative, intimating no more than that we should bear the things of God in mind as carefully as if they were bound between our eyes, distinguishes a gracious ambition to be holier than others from a proud one to appear so, and answers that the chief places are not themselves condemned, since somebody must sit uppermost.

Clarke ranks the three forms of the title as degrees of comparison, rabh great, rabbi greater and rabban greatest, and reports that the second Rabbi is omitted by several good manuscripts and most of the ancient versions; Wesley says they supposed the written scrolls a kind of charm against danger, and notes that the fringes were commanded to remind them of doing all the commandments.

Ellicott says our Lord fixes, as in the Sermon on the Mount, on the love of man applause as the thing that vitiated the highest ethical teaching and the most rigorous outward holiness, finds a special edge in the fact that many among the chief rulers were convinced of his claims yet afraid to confess him, prefers the first places nearest the host to the rendering rooms, and locates the synagogue seats at the upper end where the ark stood, assigned by the elders to those most conspicuous for devotion to the law and so coveted as a mark of religious reputation; Barnes derives the name of the frontlet from a word signifying to keep or guard, the things being worn as amulets supposed to defend from evil, and corrects the word rooms by the custom of reclining on couches ranged about three sides of a square; Robertson adds that each strip was to be tied with a well-washed hair from a calf tail lest thread or wool breed a growth that would pollute it, calls the appetite for the chief seats an insatiable hunger for prominence, and recalls that the apostles fell into an ugly quarrel over precedence at the last supper two days after hearing this; Lightfoot gives the Jewish side, the four places of the law written on labels called tephillin and fastened to the forehead and the left arm, the forehead one most conspicuous and so made broad, quotes the rule that a man may pass a synagogue during prayers if he has them on his head because they show he is studious of the law, and shows the title to be late, the worthier times having had no need of it since Hillel came up out of Babylon without it.

debates.question: Is the fault in the ornaments and the seats themselves?

sides.position: no; the places are not condemned but the loving of them, since somebody must sit uppermost
no; the fault is the motive, the love of man applause, which vitiates even rigorous holiness
the enlarging is the fault, the broadened phylactery and the longer fringe being worn to seem more religious than other men

debates.question: What were the phylacteries thought to do?

sides.position: guard the wearer, being worn as amulets against evil
show that the wearer was studious of the law, which is why the forehead one was made broad

outliers: Robertson alone preserves the rule that the parchment strips be tied with a washed hair from a calf tail, lest wool or thread breed a polluting growth.
Lightfoot alone dates the title Rabbi, showing that Hillel and the prophets were named without it and that it began with the presidents of the council.
themes: religion done where it can be seen
an ornament enlarged to be noticed
the best seat as a mark of piety
a title that belongs to one only

8.pericope_label: Be not ye called Rabbi, for one is your Master and all ye are brethren; call no man your father upon the earth; neither be ye called masters; he that is greatest among you shall be your servant, and whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased

schools.summary: Gill reads the ban as aimed at the thing rather than the word, that they were not to think themselves men of authority with dominion over the faith of others and power to bind consciences at pleasure, allows both the man who truly is greatest, having more grace and larger gifts, and the man who merely wants to be, and lays down that he who would be most esteemed ought to do the most work; Calvin refuses to divide the word father between flesh and spirit, since an apostle twice calls himself a father, locates the fault exactly in that the honour is falsely ascribed to men when it obscures the glory of God, and says the conclusion shows Christ was not disputing about words after the manner of the sophists but looking at the fact, that the highest honour in the church is not government but service, so that a man who keeps within that limit takes nothing from God whatever title he bears.

Henry quotes the rabbinic maxim that he who salutes his teacher without calling him Rabbi provokes the divine Majesty to depart from Israel, and answers that respect is commendable in the man who gives it and abominable in the man who demands it.

Clarke dates the title closely, no prophet having borne it and no Jewish doctor before Hillel and Shammai, whose rival schools had divided the people between two infallible teachers, so that the Pharisees took up a title then newly in vogue and trained their followers to use it, and suspects in the second prohibition an allusion to the Ab of the Sanhedrin, inferring that no second after Christ was to be set up in a church of which he alone is head. Wesley observes that no sentence of our Lord is repeated so often as the saying about exalting and humbling oneself, standing with scarcely a variation ten times in the evangelists.

Robertson calls the passage an apparent aside to the disciples, with the pronoun thrown forward for emphasis, quotes an old Greek commentator to the effect that one is forbidden to seek the name and not blamed if others use it, adds that father was not then a common address to a living person but a title of honour for great men of the past, and declines to read the sentence as forbidding a child his own father; Barnes puts the reason positively, that they were brethren on a level and equal in authority so that nothing was to be done which might lead the world to suppose there were ranks and grades among them, defines the word father by what it carries, authority and eminence and a right to command, which belongs eminently to God, explains the Jewish appetite for it by the notion that a teacher formed the man and gave him real life, and says God will honour the man who seeks a lowly place; Ellicott grants the beauty of the word father in its true use, where the relation of scholar and teacher was filial on one side and paternal on the other, and says it was dangerous precisely because the idea was noble, then traces the parallel in Christendom, Abbot from Abba, Papa and Pope risen from a name once given to every priest, and the English Father in God for bishops, while warning that a slavish literalism would be no better, and weighs two senses of the clause about greatness, a law of retribution by which the man who grasps at being greatest ends as servant of all, or the law which our Lord own life best illustrated, that real greatness shows itself in ministration rather than in assertion, preferring the second.

debates.question: Does the prohibition forbid the words or the thing?

sides.position: the thing, namely dominion over the faith of others and the binding of consciences
the seeking of the name; a man is not blamed if others use it of him
the titles too, so far as they imply rank among brethren who are on a level
the conventional use of a word whose true sense is noble, though a slavish literalism would be as bad

debates.question: How is the greater of them the servant?

sides.position: by a law of retribution, the man who seeks to be greatest ending as servant of all
by the nature of the case, since the highest honour in the church is service and not government
by the measure of work, he who would be most esteemed doing the most for others

outliers: Clarke alone reads the ban on the name father as an allusion to the second officer of the Sanhedrin, and so as a refusal of any second head in the church.
Ellicott alone follows the abuse of the title through the later history of Christendom, from Abbot to Pope to Father in God.
themes: a title newly fashionable in that generation
brethren on a level
a word noble in itself and dangerous in use
greatness measured by service

13.pericope_label: Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, for ye shut up the kingdom of heaven against men; ye neither go in yourselves, neither suffer ye them that are entering to go in

schools.summary: Gill observes that the men addressed had not withdrawn after their confusion but were still about him watching for an advantage, counts the woe as pronounced no less than eight times and reads it as expressing abhorrence of their wickedness, commiseration of their case and their certain destruction together, and enters a caveat that what men can shut is not eternal happiness itself, the entrance to which no man opens or shuts; Calvin says they are cursed because the government of the church was in their hands and they turned it to the destruction of the people, since doctrine is the door by which men enter life and the keys were committed to pastors for admitting them, gathers from the parallel phrase in Luke that the guardians of the law had robbed the people of its true understanding, and adds that the Papists forge keys of their own as if these had some magical power apart from the word of God.

Henry hears the woes as claps of thunder from Sinai, set deliberately against the eight beatitudes and the more dreadful for coming from one who came to bless and loved to bless, since a woe from Christ is a woe without remedy, adds that hypocrite primarily means a stage-player in religion, a man acting the part of one he neither is nor would be, and sets against the charge what they ought to have done, opened the prophecies that pointed to the Messiah and shown that Daniel weeks were expiring and the sceptre departed from Judah, whereas they pressed a ceremonial law then vanishing and suppressed the prophecies then being fulfilled; they would not enter, he says, because they were too proud to stoop to his meanness, repentance being the door and nothing more disagreeable to men who admired themselves.

Clarke keeps the disputed verse about widows houses but reverses its order with this one, reporting that the transposition is supported by some of the best manuscripts, versions and fathers, and that the critic whose edition first omitted the verse restored it in his second edition transposed exactly so; Wesley counts eight woes against the eight blessings of the mount and insists on the tone, that these are not imprecations but solemn and compassionate declarations of the misery such stubborn sinners were bringing on themselves.

Ellicott doubts our English rendering of the interjection altogether, since the Greek is capable of sorrow as well as indignation, and suggests woe for you as the better phrase; he identifies the key as the symbol handed to each scribe on his admission to office and says the only use they made of it was to lock the door, neither entering into the inner meaning of the Law and the Prophets themselves nor letting in those who were entering; Barnes calls it the most appalling discourse ever delivered to mortals, spoken in the temple before multitudes and standing as the last of his public teaching, and itemises the means of the shutting, false teaching about the Messiah, the binding of the people to tradition, and the open argument that Jesus was an impostor, by which many who were on the point of entering were turned back; Robertson traces the word hypocrite through its history, from answering to taking a part on the stage and so by an easy step to feigning and wearing a mask, notes that this hardest word from the lips of Jesus falls on the religious leaders of the nation, and counts seven woes rather than eight, the extra one being a gloss drawn from the other two Gospels which the manuscripts that keep it cannot place consistently.

debates.question: How many woes are there?

sides.position: eight, answering the eight beatitudes
seven; the verse on widows houses is a gloss from the other Gospels, and the manuscripts that keep it cannot agree where to put it
eight, but in a different order, the two verses being transposed on good manuscript authority

debates.question: What is the kingdom they shut, and what is the key?

sides.position: the church on earth, shut by false teaching about the Messiah and by pressing tradition
the door of sound doctrine, the keys being committed to pastors for admitting men to life
not eternal happiness itself, the entrance to which no man can open or shut

outliers: Ellicott alone questions the English word woe, finding the Greek interjection capable of grief as well as anger.
Gill alone limits the charge by denying that men can shut the door of salvation at all.
themes: a blessing turned into its opposite
a key used only to lock
teachers who would not go in themselves
repentance as the door they could not stoop to

14.pericope_label: Woe unto you, for ye devour widows houses and for a pretence make long prayers; woe unto you, for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves

schools.summary: Gill marks only that the same character is repeated with a fresh reason; Calvin says Christ does not merely charge them with open crimes but tears away the disguise of a virtue, since the holier a man is the more he is given to prayer, so that their case is the worse, they being so impure that the chief part of the worship of God could not be used by them without sin, and selling their prayers as hirelings dispose of their daily labour; he grants that the gaining of converts would have been a holy work in itself, but holds that to bring strangers into a worship by then degenerate was to hurry them from one danger into a greater.

Henry refuses to let the censure fall on length of prayer itself, since the cloak must be thick that could cover such practices and Christ himself continued a whole night in prayer, and finds the fault in a stated form said over by tale and used for a pretence, so that while they seemed to soar heavenward their eye was on some widow house that lay convenient; he adds that the plea which disguises sin now will aggravate the condemnation, there being degrees of damnation.

Clarke treats the opening phrase of the second woe as proverbial, like leaving no stone unturned, reports that the word rendered twofold has been shown to mean rather more deceitful, and glosses son of hell as one who might claim hell for his mother.

Barnes takes the word houses for property of any kind and finds two methods of the fraud, a reputation for exact justice to the poor which induced widows to make them guardians and executors of estates they then defrauded, and an appearance of sanctity which drew gifts from weak women under pretence of religious uses, reports that their devotions ran to three hours, distinguishes the two classes of convert, the proselyte of righteousness who was circumcised and kept the whole law and the proselyte of the gate who renounced the pagan rites without being circumcised, and says the Pharisees sought them to swell their numbers or to extort their money, taking no pains afterwards to instruct or restrain them; Ellicott offers the same pair of methods in the terms of the time, that as the jurists and notaries of the day they could press unjust claims against wealthy widows or get themselves made their heirs, and that devout women were taught that the maintenance of a scribe was the best use of wealth, identifies the long prayer with the standard series of eighteen, and recalls that the zeal of the earlier Pharisees had been a propagandism closer to the spread of the religion of Mahomet than of the gospel, John Hyrcanus having offered the Idumeans death, exile or circumcision, so that when Rome made force impossible they fell back on persuasion and exulted over a single heathen enrolled; Robertson narrows the charge, that what was made was a convert to Pharisaism rather than to Judaism, few even of the full proselytes becoming Pharisees, and judges the effort a comparative failure whose successes were worse than its failures; Lightfoot exhibits one of the arguments forged on the anvil of their covetousness, a ruling that because the Lord commanded an ark of shittim wood to be made the fellow citizens of a disciple of the wise are bound to do his servile work for him, says they angled with a double hook, for respect and by respect for gain, and quotes the rabbis against their own converts, that proselytes hinder the coming of the Messiah and are as a scab to Israel, while the more they could draw over the more purses there were to fish in.

debates.question: Are the long prayers themselves condemned?

sides.position: no; the cloak must be thick that could cover such practices, and Christ himself prayed all night
the prayer is the aggravation, since the holiest men pray most and these sold their prayers for gain
the length is a fact of their practice, the devotions running to three hours or to the standard eighteen prayers

debates.question: Why were proselytes sought, and why were they worse?

sides.position: to swell their numbers and to extort money, after which they were neither instructed nor restrained
because the convert was made to Pharisaism rather than to Judaism, so that success was worse than failure
because a worship by then degenerate could only carry the convert from one danger into a greater

outliers: Lightfoot alone quotes the rabbis own verdict that proselytes are a scab to Israel and hinder the coming of the Messiah, which the party nevertheless went on making.
Ellicott alone sets the earlier Pharisaic zeal beside a forced conversion offered by a Maccabean ruler at the point of the sword.
themes: a trade in the houses of the defenceless
prayer used as a cover
a convert won for a party
success worse than failure

16.pericope_label: Woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say whosoever shall swear by the temple it is nothing but whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple he is a debtor; ye fools and blind, for whether is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifieth the gold

schools.summary: Gill says the men who professed to guide the blind were blind themselves, ignorant of God in Christ, of the true Messiah and of the spirituality of the law, their minds darkened by an insatiable covetousness, treats the clause about the altar as a quotation of their own maxim, an oath by it being reckoned either no sin at all or no obligation, and enters the caution that Christ is not allowing any of these oaths, having forbidden them elsewhere, but telling a man what he has invoked; Calvin states the mechanism of the corruption, that the world has a natural propensity to error but that improper modes of worship gain a footing only when those in authority confirm them, such men not merely conniving at errors which are a source of gain to them but helping to fan the flame, and leads the question back to its source, that it is lawful to swear by no name but God, so that the temple may be sworn by only as the sanctuary where his glory shines, God permitting himself to be called as witness through such symbols of his presence provided no divinity is ascribed to them.

Henry finds it sad that so many should be under the guidance of men who undertake to show others a way they are themselves willingly ignorant of, and recalls the prophet watchmen who are blind while the people love to have it so.

Clarke makes the point from what an oath presupposes, a witness able to punish perjury, so that whether a man swore by the temple or the gold, the altar or the gift, he had invoked the God of all four, who would punish him even in the cases they had exempted; Wesley reads the change of title as deliberate, the first naming their personal character and the second their influence upon others, and spells out what the altar carries with it, not the gift only but the holy fire and the sacrifice, and above all the God to whom these belong, since every oath by a creature is an implicit appeal to him.

Ellicott reaches the ground of the distinction by reasoning about the casuistry itself, that coin or bullion given to the treasure had received a more special consecration than the fabric, and compares the popular feeling which makes an oath binding only when the Book is kissed, or the later Christendom that found a saint relics holier than the Gospels; Barnes puts the reply as a simple inversion, that the gold had no holiness except what the temple gave it and would be no holier than any other gold elsewhere, so that the greater thing cannot be the one deriving its sanctity from the less, that the altar likewise sanctifies the gift, and that in the end every man who swears at all swears by God or his oath is worth nothing; Robertson points out that this third woe drops the usual address altogether, that the name blind guides had already been used of them earlier in the Gospel, that the word debtor means a man owes his oath, and that the word fools is used here of their stupidity although it had been forbidden in anger, which shows that not the word but the spirit in which it is uttered is what matters; Lightfoot identifies the gold not as that shining in the walls and ceilings but as the gold offered in the sacred treasury, and explains the practice, that to swear by the temple or by the altar was so common as to be esteemed nothing and thought scarcely binding, whereas a man who swore by the treasury supposed himself tied indispensably.

debates.question: Why was the gold held more binding than the temple?

sides.position: because the gold meant was that offered in the sacred treasury, an oath by which they took for an indispensable tie
because coin or bullion given to the treasure was thought more specially consecrated than the fabric
because the covetous man gives the first place in his heart to gold, and such errors stand only where the rulers confirm them

debates.question: Are the oaths they invented binding at all?

sides.position: yes, because an oath presupposes a witness who can punish perjury, so the God of temple and altar was invoked in every case
yes, because whoever swears at all swears by God, and otherwise the oath is worth nothing
the oaths are unlawful to begin with, Christ having forbidden them elsewhere; he is telling a man what he has invoked, not approving the form

outliers: Robertson alone notices that this woe omits the standing address to scribes and Pharisees, and that the rebuke fools is used here of stupidity rather than in anger.
Calvin alone makes the people superstition the fault of their rulers, who fan errors they find profitable.
themes: guides who cannot see
a distinction drawn where the money lay
the greater thing sanctifying the less
every oath an appeal to God

23.pericope_label: Woe unto you, for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy and faith; ye blind guides, which strain at a gnat and swallow a camel

schools.summary: Gill makes the contrast the hinge of the hypocrisy, strictness in trifling ceremonies that gained them credit alongside the neglect of internal religion; Calvin reads the closing clause of the first verse as forestalling a calumny, since they might have charged him with making light of what God enjoined, grants that no part of the law may be omitted, holds that they overturn the natural order who begin with the smallest matters when the chief ones should have come first, the lesser being a kind of appendage, and that the commandments are so interwoven that none may be detached from the rest, and states what the proverb is for, the affected scrupulousness of men who shrink from a very small fault as though one transgression were more revolting than a hundred deaths while permitting themselves the most heinous crimes, which is as absurd as straining out a crumb and swallowing a whole loaf.
Henry holds that the weightiest commands are those most expressive of inward holiness, and suspects their niceness in tithing was meant to excuse the omission of these to men.

Clarke takes the three words singly, judgment as equity toward all men, mercy as kindness to the distressed and miserable, and faith as trust in God as the fountain of righteousness, says they neither began nor ended their works in God but did them to be seen of men and had their reward in human applause, and charges the familiar wording of the proverb with being an error of the press, At standing for Out in the edition of 1611 and continued ever since, producing older English Bibles which read strain out; Wesley adds only that it is strange so glaring a false print should run through all the editions.

Ellicott notes that the law names only corn and wine and oil among the produce of the earth, so that the gathering of the tenth sprig of every herb rested on a wider phrase elsewhere, and says that done at the bidding of an imperfectly illumined conscience it is not blamed, since unlike the teaching about oaths it was no perversion of the law; on the proverb he dissents from the others, holding that there is scarcely evidence enough for the printer blunder and that it is not probable in itself, and draws attention to what the two creatures have in common, the camel being named not merely as a vast thing but as an unclean beast forbidden for food; Barnes reckons that by law nearly a third of a Jew property went to religious uses, identifies the three plants as herbs of little value, the first being strewn on floors for its fragrance, says the familiar wording of the proverb is a misprint which leaves the verse without sense since the Greek means to strain a thing out through cloth or sieve, and explains the point by natural history, the gnat beginning as a grub in stagnant water which anyone nice about his drink would filter away; Robertson agrees that tithing itself is not condemned and quotes the tale in the Talmud of a rabbi ass so trained that it refused corn of which the tithes had not been taken, then presses the common ground of the two creatures, both being ceremonially unclean, and quotes the rabbinic saying that he who kills a flea on the sabbath is as guilty as if he had killed a camel; Lightfoot gives the general rule as the rabbis state it, that whatever serves for food and grows out of the earth is to be tithed, and observes that the tithing of garden herbs was an addition of the scribes which our Saviour nevertheless approved when he said these ought not to have been left undone.

debates.question: Is the familiar reading strain at a gnat a printer error?

sides.position: yes; the Greek means to strain out, and the earlier English Bibles read so
the rendering should be strain out, but there is scarcely evidence enough for a printer blunder and it is not probable in itself

debates.question: Is the tithing of herbs itself blamed?

sides.position: no; it was an addition of the scribes which our Saviour approved, saying these ought not to have been left undone
no, so far as it came of an imperfectly illumined conscience, since unlike their teaching on oaths it perverted nothing
no, but the order is wrong; to begin with the smallest matters is to overturn the natural order of the law

outliers: Ellicott alone defends the received English wording against the charge of a printer blunder.
Robertson alone brings the two halves of the proverb together by noting that gnat and camel were both ceremonially unclean.
themes: a tenth sprig of every herb
judgment, mercy and faith left undone
a filtered drink and a swallowed camel
one misprint in all our Bibles

25.pericope_label: Woe unto you, for ye make clean the outside of the cup and platter but within they are full of extortion and excess; cleanse first that which is within; woe unto you, for ye are like whited sepulchres, outwardly righteous and within full of hypocrisy and iniquity

schools.summary: Gill gathers up the whole chapter in the application, the broadened phylacteries, the enlarged borders, the long prayers, the sea and land compassed for a proselyte, the tithed herbs and the scoured cup, as the several things by which they looked outwardly beautiful; Calvin puts the absurdity of the first figure plainly, that it would be ridiculous to feast the eyes on outward splendour and then drink out of a cup full of dregs, and treats the second as the same lesson in another form, since a tomb built with beauty and splendour draws the eyes of men while inwardly it holds a stinking carcass.
Henry sharpens the first figure, that the foolishness lies in washing the side which is only looked at and leaving dirty the side which is used.

Clarke says they were exceedingly exact in the purifications the law prescribed and gave no attention to the inward purity those rites typified, reports that the manuscripts offer a whole string of words for what the cup was full of, rapine, intemperance, injustice, uncleanness, covetousness and iniquity, remarking that if one puts them all together the character of the Pharisee will not be overcharged, and turns the last verse on the reader, asking what the fair reputation acquired among men will avail when God sits in judgment upon the soul; Wesley finds the censure double, since they procured unjustly what they then used immoderately, so that luxury punished the fraud which fed it, and widens the second word past eating and drinking to every immoderate desire, of honour or gain as much as of pleasure.

Ellicott adds that the outside named in the first figure includes the inner surface, so that contents pure in their source and their use make the whole clean without any washing of the surface at all, gives the reason for the whitening of graves, that contact brought ceremonial defilement so the warning was annual and public as a leper warned passers-by with his own cry, notes that the word means smeared with lime powder, and corrects the last word of the passage, which is better rendered lawlessness, a reckless disregard of the very law they professed to interpret; Barnes states the remedy as Christ gives it, that the vessel be filled with the fruits of honest industry, after which outside and inside will both be clean; Robertson treats the accusation as the gravest yet, these punctilious observers of ceremony not hesitating at robbery and graft, calls it a picture of wickedness in high places both civil and ecclesiastical, and places the graves exactly, those of the poor in the fields and by the roadside rather than the rock-hewn tombs of the well-to-do, freshly done a month before the passover; Lightfoot distinguishes the two kinds of grave the rabbis knew, the deep one that cannot be recognised and the painted one that is meant to be seen, observes that our Lord uses the first in the other Gospel and the second here, quotes the tradition that on the fifteenth of Adar they repaired the roads and the sewers and marked the graves with chalk tempered in water, and supplies the Jewish name for such men, the distained or coloured, with the deathbed warning of Jannai the king to his wife to beware of painted men pretending to be Pharisees, whose works are the works of Zimri while they expect the reward of Phineas.

debates.question: What does cleansing the inside first accomplish?

sides.position: it makes the outside clean too, the vessel being filled with the fruits of honest industry
it is the whole of it, since contents pure in source and use leave nothing for a surface washing to do
it reverses a folly, the washing of the side that is looked at and the leaving of the side that is used

debates.question: Which grave is the comparison drawn from?

sides.position: the painted or marked grave, whitened once a year so that passers-by might avoid defilement
the tomb built with beauty and splendour, which draws the eye while holding a carcass

outliers: Clarke alone turns the whole passage on the reader with a direct charge to see that his own heart is right with God.
Lightfoot alone preserves the Jewish word for such men, the distained or coloured, and the dying king warning against painted Pharisees.
themes: a vessel scoured on the side that shows
the fruits of honest industry
graves marked so men may avoid them
lawlessness under a righteous surface

29.pericope_label: Woe unto you, for ye build the tombs of the prophets and say if we had been in the days of our fathers we would not have been partakers; fill ye up then the measure of your fathers; ye serpents, ye generation of vipers, how can ye escape the damnation of hell

schools.summary: Gill supplies the measure itself, the bounds set to a nation sin, which their fathers had carried far and which these sons would fill brimful by crucifying the Son of God; Calvin rejects the reading that takes the tomb-building for superstition in honouring the dead with splendid monuments, since they had not yet reached that pitch of blindness, and finds instead a bid for the favour of the ignorant multitude, by which they passed for faithful imitators of the prophets and keen zealots for the worship of God, finds a double folly in their disclaimer, that the honour paid to the dead was treated as a kind of expiation for the fathers guilt and that men descended from the bloody enemies of God should boast of a sacred ancestry, and denies that the command to fill up bids them do anything, reading it figuratively, that this cruelty is the ancient discipline of the nation and almost natural to them, so that they must be left to finish the web their fathers began.

Henry calls the tomb-building the varnish, contrasts it with the older reverence of the king who thought it respect enough to leave a prophet bones unmoved, and says in his own figure that patience abused turns into the greatest wrath, the longer the treasures of wickedness are heaped up the fuller the treasures of wrath will be.

Clarke allows that they thought themselves much better than their ancestors and turns the mirror round, that many suppose had they lived then they would not have done as those men did, which is hard to believe of people who reject the gospel and hate its followers now, reaches the sense of the imperative by grammar, the form standing for the future after a Hebrew idiom as when the temple is bidden be destroyed, and fixes the phrase about the generation on the race of men then living, a sense the word often carries in the Gospels.

Ellicott points to four conspicuous monuments still standing at the base of the Mount of Olives, whose mixture of debased Doric and Egyptian work belongs to the Herodian period, and suggests these may be the sepulchres meant, sees no need to assume that the Pharisees did not mean what they said, taking it for the unconscious hypocrisy of which every generation is guilty when it condemns the bigotry or greed of the past and then yields to the same sins itself, and makes the imputation depend on the imitation, men making the guilt of past ages their own and reproducing its atrocities until what looks like an arbitrary decree becomes a righteous judgment, while repentance would cut off the entail; Barnes reads the imperative as prediction, a statement of what they were about to do, completes the sense from what follows, that by slaying him they would make the national guilt full, puts the weight of the verse about witnesses on the two words unto yourselves, making it an appeal to conscience since under all the profession they knew that they approved in their hearts the deed they disowned with their lips, and dates the fulfilment about forty years from the speaking; Robertson adds that some of the four monuments may have been going up at the very hour Jesus spoke, observes that in this last woe he addresses the nation and not the Pharisees only, calls the command to fill up the keenest irony and notes that some manuscripts have softened it into a plain future, and finds the closing words so blistering that they cut like whip-cords, quoting a curse of the same shape from the Talmud upon the house of Annas.

debates.question: Why did they build and garnish the tombs?

sides.position: out of professed veneration, as men in the East still build a tomb to honour a distinguished name
to win the favour of the multitude, who would take them for faithful imitators of the prophets; it was not superstition about the dead
as a varnish over the persecution of living prophets

debates.question: In what sense are they told to fill up the measure?

sides.position: as a prediction of what they were about to do in slaying him
as a future expressed by an imperative, after a Hebrew idiom
as the keenest irony, which some manuscripts have softened into a plain future
as permission rather than command, Christ contending with them no longer
as neither, but a figure for a hereditary cruelty they must be left to carry through

outliers: Ellicott alone declines to call their disclaimer insincere, treating it as the unconscious hypocrisy of every generation that condemns the past and then repeats it.
Clarke alone turns the disclaimer on the reader, doubting that men who reject the gospel now would have acted otherwise then.
themes: monuments to the men their fathers killed
a disclaimer that condemns the speaker
a measure filled to the brim
words that cut like whip-cords

34.pericope_label: Behold I send unto you prophets and wise men and scribes, and some of them ye shall kill and crucify and some ye shall scourge and persecute, that upon you may come all the righteous blood shed upon the earth from Abel to Zacharias; all these things shall come upon this generation

schools.summary: Gill marks the solemn preface as the usual form for raising attention to something of moment; Calvin grants the objection that children should not be punished for their parents sins and answers it by conspiracy, that since the whole nation through every age is involved in one rebellion it is not strange that the punishment owed to the fathers should fall on the children.

Henry remarks on the strangeness of the connection, that after calling them a brood of vipers one would expect him to say they should never have a prophet again, whereas he says therefore he will send them prophets, either that they may yet be wrought upon or that they may be left inexcusable, notes that the sending is itself a claim since to gift and commission prophets is an act of kingly office, begins the tally of blood where the text does, with Abel, finding it striking that the first man to die died for his religion, and says that patience abused turns into the greatest wrath.

Clarke identifies the messengers with the evangelists, apostles and deacons who were to equal the ancient prophets in the gifts of the Spirit, reads the threat precisely, that some they would kill by legal process and some they would try and find guilty and hand to the Romans who through them would put the men to death, and fixes the closing phrase on the race of men then living, a sense the word often carries in the Gospels; Wesley hears the claim of authority in the bare words and distinguishes the three titles, prophets as men with supernatural credentials, wise men as those having natural ability and experience, and scribes as men of learning, adding that none of it would avail.

Ellicott states the difficulty against the usual identification of the murdered Zacharias, since the man stoned in the court of the house of the Lord was the son of Jehoiada while the only son of Barachias in the older books is the minor prophet, of whose death nothing is known and whose murder in such a manner would hardly have gone unrecorded, adds that the earlier death had gathered legends, the Talmud saying that the blood would not dry up, and makes the imputation of guilt depend on the imitation, men making the guilt of past ages their own and reproducing its atrocities until what looks like an arbitrary decree becomes a righteous judgment, while repentance would cut off the entail; Barnes names the fulfilments of the threat, Stephen killed and James, the scourging recorded in the Acts and by the apostle himself, observes that the Jews had no power of crucifixion but gave their victims into Roman hands, draws the distinction about inherited guilt more narrowly, that God did not hold them guilty of what their fathers did but that temporal judgments descend on children through a parent wickedness as a drunken father wastes the property his children might have had, and dates the fulfilment about forty years from the speaking; Robertson accepts the usual identification of Zacharias and admits the rest frankly, that how the words son of Barachiah entered this Gospel we do not know and that half a dozen possibilities may be suggested; Lightfoot argues at length for the Zacharias killed by king Joash, on the grounds that no other of the name is said to have been slain before these words were spoken, that his death in the temple is related in express words, and that the Jews made it memorable by a signal revenge.

debates.question: Which Zacharias is meant?

sides.position: the son of Jehoiada, killed by king Joash; no other of the name is recorded as slain, and the Jews made that death memorable
that identification leaves the patronymic unexplained, since the only son of Barachias in the older books is the minor prophet, of whose death nothing is known
the identification stands, but how the words son of Barachiah entered the text we do not know

debates.question: How can this generation bear the guilt of all the blood?

sides.position: because the whole nation in every age is involved in one conspiracy, so the punishment owed the fathers falls on the children
not as personal guilt; temporal judgments descend on children through a parent wickedness, and the crimes being national the judgment is national
because they make the guilt of past ages their own by imitation, so that the decree is righteous and repentance would cut off the entail

outliers: Ellicott alone presses the objection that the patronymic fits none of the recorded martyrdoms.
Henry alone dwells on the strangeness of promising prophets to a generation just sentenced, as a sending that leaves them either won or inexcusable.
themes: messengers sent to a condemned generation
prophets, wise men and scribes
a reckoning from the first martyr
guilt inherited by imitation

37.pericope_label: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, how often would I have gathered thy children as a hen gathereth her chickens, and ye would not; behold your house is left unto you desolate, for ye shall not see me henceforth till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord

schools.summary: Gill takes the address to fall not on the buildings but on the inhabitants, and among these chiefly on the rulers and the great council, since it belonged to them to examine men who claimed to be prophets and to condemn those they judged false; Calvin says the city God had chosen for his own habitation had shown itself unworthy of the honour and, like a den of robbers, had grown accustomed to suck the blood of the prophets, the repeated name marking an impiety that deserves no ordinary detestation and the charge being not one murder or two but a custom deeply rooted, explains the confidence that made the threat incredible to them, that they thought God bound to the place he had chosen for his only habitation in the world and treated the temple as an invincible fortress as if they dwelt in the bosom of God, and rejects both the reading that defers everything to the last judgment and the reading that finds the closing words fulfilled soon after, taking them of men who will find their Judge in the Redeemer they despised and who even now sing that very psalm daily while scorning him whom it names.

Henry sets the two occasions side by side, that a day or two before he had wept over the city and now he sighed over it, plays on the name, the vision of peace becoming the seat of war and confusion, and presses what the wings are for, protection and safety on the one hand and warmth and comfort on the other, so that souls have in Christ both refuge and refreshment.

Clarke draws a doctrine from the figure of the hen, that our Lord seriously wished the salvation of these people and did everything which could be done consistently with his own perfections and the liberty of his creatures, his tears over the city proving his sincerity, so that if they perished the reason was their refusal to be gathered, and adds the natural picture, the hen calling her chickens together at the sight of a bird of prey that she may cover them with her wings; with Wesley he holds that the temple which had been the Lord own house is now called theirs to intimate that God had abandoned it, Wesley adding that it was spoken as he went out of it for the last time.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew form of the name stands here only in this Gospel, as though the very syllables had fixed themselves in men memories, and that the verbs are present, taking in the past and the future together with a sad foresight of what lay in store for his own messengers, and refers the welcome of the last verse to the second Advent and to the true Israel of God, holding that for that generation and for the outward Israel the abandonment was final; Barnes holds that the day of mercy is gone by until the judgments have been borne, but that the days will come when the long-rejected nation will hail Jesus as the Messiah; Robertson renders the clause more exactly, how often did I long to gather them to myself, notes that the verb is the one used of the hen with her brood, and observes that the words imply earlier visits to the city such as the fourth Gospel records; Lightfoot supplies what the rabbis themselves said of the city record, that it had killed Uriah and Zechariah and Isaiah.

debates.question: When will they say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord?

sides.position: when the judgments have been borne and the long-rejected nation at last hails him as Messiah
at the second Advent, from the true Israel of God; for that generation and the outward Israel the abandonment was final
neither at the last judgment in the usual sense nor soon after; the words will be wrung from men who find their Judge in the Redeemer they despised

debates.question: Whose house is left desolate?

sides.position: the temple, called theirs rather than his to signify that God has abandoned it
the city and the temple together, which within some forty years would be a desert
the fortress of their confidence, which they thought God bound to and could not leave

outliers: Clarke alone builds a doctrine of the will of Christ out of the figure, that men have perished whom he wished and bled to save.
Calvin alone reads the closing acclamation as a confession wrung from the condemned rather than a welcome from the converted.
themes: a name repeated in grief
a hen and a bird of prey
a house handed back to its owners
a welcome that comes too late or not at all
